assessments.task_description:
This course demands a serious commitment to reading. Please set aside dedicated time each week to engage with the required readings as carefully and slowly as possible.

Each week, in tutorials, starting in Week 2, there will be a timed writing exercise that must be completed on the provided worksheet. You are not permitted to access devices of any kind during the task, but may consult printed or handwritten notes. You are responsible for bringing your own pen or pencil.

You will be given a specific prompt for each exercise that will refer to content from the required readings and lecture, or will be related to the assessment. Tutors will collect the worksheets afterwards to record completion of the assessment task. Feedback will be given informally in the tutorial immediately after writing.

Each Weekly Tutorial Writing Exercise is worth 5 points.

You will receive 5 points for each complete and meaningful answer, 3 points for a partially complete answer, 1 point for a genuine attempt that demonstrates engagement with the question but is largely incorrect or misleading, and 0 points if your response does not address the prompt or if you leave the worksheet blank. You will also receive 0 points if you don't attend the tutorial, and if you fail to follow the instruction to put away your device during the exercise the the incident may be referred to an Integrity Officer for further investigation.

Partial marks will not be given (either you get 5 points, 3 points, 1 point, or 0 points).

There are 10 opportunities across the semester, each worth 5%. Only your best 6 results count, together forming 30% of your final grade. Because only 6 of the 10 count, the assessment already builds in the flexibility to miss up to 4 sessions — for illness or any other reason — with no penalty and no documentation required.

There are no opportunities to re-take an individual exercise, and no alternative assessment is available except in the specific circumstances set out below. As this is an internal course, you must make yourself available to complete each exercise at the scheduled date, time and venue. These are handwritten, open-book tasks, but no electronic devices may be used. Any written or printed material is permitted, and material may be annotated. All electronic devices must remain in your bag or under your desk, and must be switched off or in airplane mode. If a device emits any noise, you may be subject to an allegation of misconduct and the item may be confiscated for the duration of the exercise.

Alternative assessment and accommodations

If you have a Disability Action Plan relevant to this task, please contact the course coordinator as early as possible. Reasonable accommodations can be made for matters documented in a Disability Action Plan (for example, if you are unable to handwrite under timed conditions).

The 4-session buffer described above is intended to cover ordinary absences. A separate make-up session is available only to students who, for a genuine and documented reason, miss more than 4 of the exercises — for example, a sudden or serious illness, or another documented cause requiring a lengthy absence. Missing 4 or fewer sessions is already covered by the best-6-of-10 structure and does not qualify for a make-up.

To be considered for a make-up session or any other alternative arrangement, you must contact the course coordinator with your documentation as soon as possible after the circumstances arise. One make-up session will be offered in the Week 13 lecture slot; if you are eligible, please ensure you are available.

assessments.task_description:
In this task, students will conduct and record three interviews (in audio format) with individuals from the same sociocultural group (e.g., same age cohort, occupation, gender identity, cultural background, etc.) to explore their algorithmic imaginaries—that is, their beliefs, assumptions, and everyday "theories" about how platforms and algorithms work, affect them, and shape their online experience.

This assessment comprises four components: 

  1. You will workshop your interview plan with your tutor, including selecting appropriate participants, developing effective interview questions, and addressing relevant methodological or ethical considerations.
  2. You will conduct three (3) audio-recorded interviews (20–30 minutes each). Submit the audio files via Blackboard Assignments .
  3. You will compile a list of at least 10 potential quotes from your interviews, each with an exact timestamp and a short explanation of how it contributes to the development of your Final Essay’s central argument.
  4. You will develop a Report (1000 words) that provides an overview of the interviews, identifies key social patterns/themes across the interviews regarding algorithmic imaginaries, and interprets relevant quotes.


There will be tutorials dedicated to helping you with this assignment. You are not expected to cite scholarly works in the Report, but if you choose to do so, please use the Chicago 18th Author-Date Referencing Style.
assessments.submission_guidelines: Submit the Report via TurnItIn on Blackboard and the audio files via Blackboard Assignments.
assessments.deferral_or_extension: You may be able to apply for an extension.
assessments.late_submission: A penalty of 10% of the maximum possible mark will be deducted per 24 hours from time submission is due for up to 7 days. After 7 days, you will receive a mark of 0.
assessments.additional_info: You may be able to apply for an extension.

assessments.task_description:
Building directly on Assessment 2, this assessment requires students to work at a higher level of abstraction by synthesising theory, empirical research, and thematic analysis into a cohesive essay. Drawing on their interview data, students will critically analyse their interviewee's algorithmic imaginary and situate it within broader social, cultural, and technological contexts, making meaningful connections to the experiences and perspectives of their interviewee's wider social group.

Students are expected to draw on insights, quotes, interpretations, and reflections from their Assessment 2's Report. However, students must also extend their analysis by putting their findings into dialogue with at least ONE additional concept introduced in the course beyond the concept of "algorithmic imaginary".

The essay should critically engage with at least four scholarly sources (journal articles, books, or book chapters), with at least two of the four assigned as required readings for this course.

The essay should use Chicago 18th Author-Date Referencing Style.
